2.text: WALRUS AND WHALE HUNTING. — The long harpoon used in walrus-hunting
2.note: Run-in heading set in small capitals; keyed as plain ASCII capitals per keying_spec.md §2.13.

3.text: has the same shape as the harpoons already described; but

4.text: the end of the line has one or two floats tied to it (Fig. 38).

5.text: These are thrown into the water after a successful blow. Floats

6.text: (Fig. 39, a) consist of a whole seal-skin skilfully removed from

7.text: the carcass of the animal. The mouth is enlarged by an oblong

8.text: cut down the neck, and the skin is pulled off like a stocking.

9.text: The head is carefully sewed up, the fore-flippers often cut off, and

10.text: the openings firmly tied up. One of them is used for inflating

11.text: the float, which is done without an inflating-pipe such as is used

12.text: by the Eskimo. The skin of the hind-flippers is carefully stitched;

13.text: and when the body is inflated, the flippers stand out, furnishing

14.text: a hold for the separate loops on the end of the line (Fig. 39, b).

15.text: At the present time, however, walrus-hunting is done almost

16.text: exclusively with rifles, especially on the Pacific. Thirty years

17.text: ago American whalers applied themselves to a great extent

18.text: to walrus-hunting, and the number of walrus on the Pacific

19.text: consequently began to decrease rapidly. Later on, the whalers

20.text: desisted from the pursuit, asserting that prices were too low,

21.text: and that the whole business was not remunerative enough.

22.text: Then the decrease slackened, although even now the reckless

23.text: shooting of walrus by the natives continues to work disaster.

24.text: To the south of Anadyr the walrus have greatly diminished in

25.text: numbers. That is the reason that the Kerek on the southern

26.text: shore of Anadyr Bay, who in former times subsisted on walrus,

27.text: are now rapidly starving to death. Farther to the south walrus

28.text: became very rare in the vicinity of most of the villages, and

29.text: are now met with only on the shores of some islands, as Karagha

30.text: Island, for instance. To the north of Anadyr, beginning at

31.text: the northern shore of Holy Cross Bay, considerable numbers

32.text: of walrus are still killed. For some villages, as Miˊs˙qᴀn and
32.resolved: Miˊs˙qᴀn = M, i, U+02CA (stress), s, U+02D9 (postposed palatalization dot on s, licensed §2.1 series n x d t s č ǰ), q, U+1D00 small-cap ᴀ, n
32.note: Tier-1 toponym. Raised dot after s read as postposed palatalization mark (s˙), matching the licensed series. Final letters after q: an elevated capital-height glyph read as small-cap ᴀ (U+1D00, licensed §2.3), followed by ordinary lowercase n (confirmed at 4x against the following word 'and' on the same line, same x-height). First vowel keyed plain dotted 'i': at 4x it clearly carries a separate round tittle above the stem, distinct from and to the left of the stress mark, which reads as ordinary dotted i rather than the dotless small-cap ɪ. `lexicon lookup sqan` was consulted and surfaces the same toponym (in the same Holy Cross Bay context) keyed `Mɪˊs˙qᴀn` in ground truth on 1-048 — a real contradiction the raster here does not resolve in that direction. Flagging for adjudication rather than adopting the other page's spelling.

35.text: On the Pacific shore the walrus is killed chiefly during its migrations

36.text: from Holy Cross Bay to East Cape and back again (Plate X, Figs. 1, 3).
